newsitem.title: UK: Pause or not, UK rates are likely to head higher.
newsitem.headline: Pause or not, UK rates are likely to head higher.

text.p: British interest rates may be on hold, according to the Bank of England, but with unemployment at record lows and high street shops basking in near-boom conditions, they have further to rise, economists said on Wednesday.
Official figures out on Wednesday showed the number of Britons out of work -- 1.55 million in July -- was the lowest in 17 years.
Annual average earnings growth held steady at 4.25 percent in June, so there was little immediate inflationary threat from the jobs figures.

But with unemployment falling relentlessly -- July's drop was the 17th in succession -- wage pressures are bound to pick up soon. Add to that an already-frantic pace of high street spending and few experts expect rates to peak at seven percent.
"The Monetary Policy Committee will be concerned that unemployment cannot keep falling this fast without wage pressures eventually emerging," said Jonathan Loynes, UK economist at HSBC Markets.
"Accordingly, while rates are on hold for a while, they have probably not yet reached a peak."
A couple of hours after the jobs data were released, the Bank of England said rates have risen far enough to allow pause for thought.

After four quarter-point increases in as many months, base rates now stand at seven percent, and may be high enough for the government's 2.5 percent target for underlying inflation to be met in two years time, the Bank said.

Bank of England chief economist Mervyn King, unveiling the Bank's quarterly inflation report in front of the television cameras for the first time, said it would want to see a substantial amount of economic data before deciding to move rates again.
The financial markets instantly speculated about how long the pause might be, or if it signalled that rates have peaked. But if King knew, he was not letting on.
"We have not decided that the next move in interest rates would be upward and that the only uncertain factor is how long we wait," he said.
Kevin Gardiner, UK economist at Morgan Stanley, said that meant a hiatus of at least three months. But he still saw base rates peaking at eight percent next year.
"We think the economy is probably stronger than the Bank believes. They talk about growth slowing down later this year, we think it will accelerate."
Consumer spending is certainly buoyant -- June retail sales were up 4.5 percent on the year -- and a flood of windfall payments from building societies converting into banks can only add to that.
The Bank estimated 36 billion pounds in free shares have been handed out and will add about one percentage point to consumption growth this year.
It has commissioned a special report on the windfall effect. But that may prove premature.
"It takes a while for people to get used to windfalls like these, and to decide how to spend them," Gardiner said. "A lot of the spending won't show up until the third quarter at least."
Ian Stewart, UK economist at Merrill Lynch, said the Bank's report, although forecasting the government's inflation target will be hit, dwelt largely on the upside risks.
"It is difficult to avoid the conclusion that they're painting a picture of an economy that is growing quite fast," he said. "The implication is they will return to tightening later this year."
One factor that could stop further policy tightening is the path the pound takes in the months ahead, a fact the Bank acknowledged.
If it sticks anywhere near to three marks then further rate rises risk a full-blown recession in the manufacturing sector as exporters are squeezed out of existence.
But if it falls, tighter monetary policy may quickly become necessary. A strong pound also cuts import prices, thereby bearing down on inflation. The further it falls, the more imported goods cost.
King said the Bank expected the pound to fall back to 90 on a trade-weighted basis within two years. It closed at 100.7 on Wednesday.
"That's quite a substantial fall," he said. "One of the downside risks to the forecast is that sterling may not fall back to that level."
Sterling has soared almost 30 percent against the mark since last August despite sliding about five pfennigs to 2.89 marks on Wednesday.

As any dealer will tell you, second-guessing the currency markets is a risky business. "Most people in the City find it tough to forecast the currency for one day to the next but at least we know what they're basing their forecasts on," said John Shepperd, chief economist at Yamaichi International.
But whatever happens to rates, it is wise to put the debate in the context of the 1980s when boom led to bust and base rates peaked at 15 percent.
"I think rates will peak at 7.5 percent but that was the trough in the last cycle. It highlights how good the inflation outlook really is," said Gerard Lyons, chief economist at DKB International.
